chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: After discussing the next day's attack with the esaul for some time—an attack that now, seeing how close they were to the French, he seemed to have definitely decided on—Denisov turned his horse and rode back.
'Come on, my lad, let's go get dry,' he said to Petya.

As they approached the watchman's hut, Denisov stopped, peering into the forest. Among the trees, a man with long legs and long, swinging arms was approaching with light, loping strides. He wore a short jacket, bast shoes, and a Kazan hat, with a musket over his shoulder and an axe stuck in his belt. When he spotted Denisov, he quickly tossed something into the bushes, pulled off his soggy hat by its floppy brim, and came up to his commander. It was Tikhon. His wrinkled, pockmarked face and narrow little eyes beamed with self-satisfied amusement. He lifted his head high and looked at Denisov as if suppressing a laugh.
'Well, where did you disappear to?' asked Denisov.
'Where did I disappear to? I went to get Frenchmen,' answered Tikhon boldly, in a husky but melodious bass.
'Why did you go pushing in there in broad daylight? You fool! So why haven't you brought one?'
'Oh, I grabbed one all right,' said Tikhon.
'Where is he?'

'Well, I nabbed one first thing at dawn,' Tikhon went on, spreading out his flat feet with their turned-out toes in their bast shoes. 'I took him into the forest. Then I had a look at him and thought: he's no good. So I decided to go fetch a better one.'
'You see?... What a rogue—just as I thought,' said Denisov to the esaul. 'Why didn't you bring that one?'
'What was the good of bringing him?' Tikhon interrupted hastily and angrily. 'That one wouldn't have done for you. Don't I know what kind you need!'
'What a brute!... Well? Go on.'

'I went for another one,' Tikhon continued. 'I crept through the woods like this and lay down.' (He suddenly dropped flat on his stomach with a supple movement to demonstrate.) 'One came along and I grabbed him, like this.' (He sprang up quickly and lightly.) '"Come along to the colonel," I said. He starts yelling, and suddenly there were four of them. They went at me with their little swords. So I laid into them with my axe, like this: "What do you think you're doing?" I shouted. "In the name of Christ!"' Tikhon yelled, waving his arms with an angry scowl, puffing out his chest.
'Yes, we saw from the hill how you ran for it through the puddles!' said the esaul, squinting with amusement.
Petya badly wanted to laugh but saw that everyone else was holding back. He looked quickly from Tikhon's face to the esaul's and Denisov's, unable to figure out what it all meant.
'Don't play the fool!' said Denisov, coughing angrily. 'Why didn't you bring the first one?'

Tikhon scratched his back with one hand and his head with the other, and then suddenly his whole face broke into a beaming, foolish grin that revealed the gap where he'd lost a tooth (which was why he was called Shcherbaty—the gap-toothed). Denisov smiled, and Petya burst into a peal of delighted laughter that Tikhon himself joined.
'Oh, but he was a complete good-for-nothing,' said Tikhon. 'The clothes on him—absolute rags! How could I bring him? And so rude, your honor! "I'm a general's son," he says, "and I won't go!"'
'You're a brute!' said Denisov. 'I needed to question him...'

'But I did question him,' said Tikhon. 'He said he didn't know much. "There are a lot of us," he says, "but we're all in poor shape—soldiers in name only. Just shout loud at them," he says, "and you'll take them all."' Tikhon concluded with a cheerful, resolute look at Denisov.
'I'll give you a hundred lashes—that'll teach you to play the fool!' said Denisov severely.
'But why are you angry?' Tikhon protested. 'Just because I haven't seen your Frenchmen before? Wait till it gets dark and I'll bring you any of them you want—three if you like.'
'Well, let's go,' said Denisov, and he rode all the way to the watchman's hut in silence, frowning angrily.
Tikhon followed behind, and Petya heard the Cossacks laughing with him and at him about some pair of boots he'd thrown into the bushes.

When the fit of laughter brought on by Tikhon's words and smile had passed, and Petya realized for a moment that this Tikhon had actually killed a man, he felt uneasy. He glanced at the captive drummer boy and felt a pang in his heart. But the uneasiness lasted only a moment. He felt he needed to hold his head higher, brace himself, and question the esaul with an air of authority about the next day's operation, so as not to be unworthy of the company he was in.
The officer sent to find out about Dolokhov met Denisov on the way with news that Dolokhov would come soon and that everything was fine.
Denisov immediately cheered up and, calling Petya over, said: 'Well, tell me about yourself.'

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter VII
paragraphs: Petya had left his family after their departure from Moscow, joined his regiment, and soon been taken on as orderly by a general commanding a large guerrilla detachment. From the time he received his commission, and especially since joining the active army and fighting at Vyazma, Petya had been in a state of perpetual, blissful excitement at being grown up, combined with a frantic eagerness not to miss any chance for real heroism. He was thrilled by everything he saw and experienced in the army, but at the same time it always seemed to him that the truly heroic feats were happening just where he wasn't. He was always in a hurry to be somewhere else.

When on the twenty-first of October his general had wanted to send someone to Denisov's detachment, Petya had begged so desperately to go that the general couldn't refuse. But remembering Petya's reckless behavior at Vyazma—where instead of riding along the road to his assigned position, he had galloped to the front line under French fire and twice discharged his pistol—the general explicitly forbade him from taking part in any of Denisov's operations. That was why Petya had blushed and grown flustered when Denisov asked if he could stay. Before they had even ridden to the forest's edge, Petya had been telling himself he must follow his orders strictly and return immediately. But when he saw the French, and saw Tikhon, and learned there would certainly be an attack that night, he decided—with the speed at which young people reverse their views—that the general he had greatly respected until now was a worthless German, that Denisov was a hero, the esaul was a hero, Tikhon was a hero too, and that it would be shameful to leave them at a moment of difficulty.

It was already getting dark when Denisov, Petya, and the esaul rode up to the watchman's hut. In the twilight, saddled horses could be seen, and Cossacks and hussars who had set up rough shelters in the clearing were lighting fires in a hollow where the French couldn't see the smoke. In the passageway of the small hut, a Cossack with rolled-up sleeves was chopping mutton. Inside, three of Denisov's officers were turning a door into a table. Petya took off his wet clothes, gave them to be dried, and immediately pitched in helping set up the dinner table.
In ten minutes the table was ready with a cloth spread on it. On the table were vodka, a flask of rum, white bread, roast mutton, and salt.

Sitting at the table with the officers, tearing apart the savory, fatty mutton with his fingers while grease ran down his hands, Petya was in an ecstatic, childlike state of love for everyone around him, and therefore of confidence that everyone loved him back.

'So what do you think, Vasili Dmitrich?' he said to Denisov. 'It's all right if I stay with you for a day?' And without waiting for an answer, he answered himself: 'You see, I was told to find things out—well, I am finding things out. Only please let me into the very thick of it... the real action... I don't want a reward. I just want...'
Petya clenched his teeth and looked around, tossing his head back and waving his arms.
'Into the very thick of it...' Denisov repeated with a smile.

'Only, please, give me a command—some real responsibility so I can actually command something,' Petya went on. 'What would it cost you? Oh, do you need a knife?' he asked, turning to an officer who wanted to cut some mutton.
And he handed over his clasp knife. The officer admired it.

'Please keep it. I've got several like it,' said Petya, blushing. 'Heavens! I almost forgot!' he suddenly cried. 'I've got raisins—wonderful ones, seedless. We have a new sutler and he has amazing stuff. I bought ten pounds. I like having something sweet. Would you like some?' And Petya ran out to his Cossack in the passage and came back with bags containing about five pounds of raisins. 'Help yourselves, gentlemen!'

'Do you need a coffeepot?' he asked the esaul. 'I bought a wonderful one from our sutler! He has fantastic things. And he's very honest—that's the main thing. I'll make sure to send it to you. Or maybe your flints are worn out or used up—that happens sometimes, you know. I brought some along, right here'—he showed a bag—'a hundred flints. I got them very cheap. Please take as many as you want—or all of them...'
Then, suddenly afraid he'd said too much, Petya stopped and blushed.

He tried to remember if he'd done anything else foolish. Running through the day's events, he thought of the French drummer boy. 'It's fine for us here, but what about him? Where have they put him? Have they fed him? Did anyone hurt his feelings?' But having already caught himself going overboard about the flints, he was afraid to speak.

'I could ask,' he thought, 'but they'll say: "He's just a boy himself, so he feels sorry for the boy." I'll show them tomorrow whether I'm a boy! Would it seem odd if I asked?' Petya wondered. 'Oh well, never mind!' And immediately, blushing and watching the officers anxiously for any sign of mockery, he said:
'May I call in that prisoner boy and give him something to eat? Maybe...'
'Yes, he's a poor little fellow,' said Denisov, who clearly saw nothing shameful in the suggestion. 'Bring him in. His name is Vincent Bosse. Go get him.'
'I'll call him,' said Petya.
'Yes, yes, go ahead. Poor little fellow,' Denisov repeated.
Petya was at the door when Denisov said this. He slipped between the officers, came close to Denisov, and said:
'Let me kiss you, dear old fellow! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid!'
And having kissed Denisov, he ran out of the hut.
'Bosse! Vincent!' Petya called, stopping outside the door.
'Who do you want, sir?' asked a voice from the darkness.
Petya said he wanted the French boy who had been captured that day.
'Ah, Vesenny?' said a Cossack.

Vincent, the boy's name, had already been transformed by the Cossacks into Vesenny (springlike) and by the peasants and soldiers into Vesenya. In both these adaptations, the echo of spring matched the impression made by the young lad.
'He's warming himself over at the bonfire. Hey, Vesenya! Vesenya! Vesenny!' laughing voices called to one another in the darkness.
'He's a smart lad,' said a hussar standing near Petya. 'We gave him something to eat a while ago. He was terribly hungry!'
The sound of bare feet splashing through mud was heard in the darkness, and the drummer boy appeared at the door.
'Ah, it's you!' said Petya. 'Are you hungry? Don't be afraid—no one will hurt you. Come in, come in.'
('Thank you, sir.')
('Come in, come in.')
'Thank you, sir,' said the drummer boy in a trembling, almost childish voice, and he began scraping his dirty feet on the threshold.
('Thank you, sir.')
There were many things Petya wanted to say to the drummer boy but didn't dare. He stood beside him in the passage, uncertain. Then, in the darkness, he took the boy's hand and squeezed it.
'Come in, come in!' he repeated in a gentle whisper. 'Oh, what can I do for him?' he thought, and opening the door, let the boy go in first.

When the boy had entered the hut, Petya sat down at a distance from him, feeling it beneath his dignity to pay him attention. But he fingered the money in his pocket and wondered whether it would seem ridiculous to give some to the drummer boy.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter VIII
paragraphs: Dolokhov's arrival diverted Petya's attention from the drummer boy—whom Denisov had already had fed with mutton and vodka and dressed in a Russian coat so he could be kept with their band rather than sent away with the other prisoners. Petya had heard many stories in the army about Dolokhov's extraordinary bravery and his cruelty toward the French. So from the moment Dolokhov entered the hut, Petya couldn't take his eyes off him, bracing himself and holding his head high to prove himself worthy of such company.
Dolokhov's appearance surprised Petya by its simplicity.

Denisov wore a Cossack coat, had a beard, carried an icon of St. Nicholas the Wonder-Worker on his chest, and everything about him signaled his unusual position. But Dolokhov, who had worn Persian garb in Moscow, now looked like a textbook Guards officer. He was clean-shaven and wore a padded Guards coat with a St. George medal at his buttonhole and a plain forage cap set straight on his head. He took off his wet felt cloak in a corner without greeting anyone, went straight to Denisov, and began questioning him about the situation. Denisov told him about the large detachments' designs on the convoy, the message Petya had brought, and his own responses to both generals. Then he told him everything he knew about the French column.

'That's fine. But we need to know exactly what troops they are and how many,' said Dolokhov. 'We'll need to go there ourselves. We can't start without knowing the precise numbers. I like to work accurately. Now—wouldn't one of these gentlemen like to ride with me to the French camp? I've brought a spare uniform.'
'I'll go! I'll go with you!' cried Petya.
'You absolutely don't need to go,' said Denisov, addressing Dolokhov, 'and as for him, I won't allow it under any circumstances.'
'I like that!' exclaimed Petya. 'Why shouldn't I go?'
'Because there's no point.'
'Well, excuse me, but... because... because... I'm going, and that's final. You'll take me, won't you?' he said, turning to Dolokhov.
'Why not?' Dolokhov answered absently, studying the French drummer boy's face. 'Have you had that youngster long?' he asked Denisov.
'He was captured today, but he doesn't know anything. I'm keeping him with us.'
'And where do you put the rest of them?' Dolokhov asked.

'Where? I send them away and get a receipt for them,' Denisov burst out, suddenly flushing. 'And I say plainly that I don't have a single man's life on my conscience. Would it really be so hard to send thirty or three hundred men to town under escort, instead of staining—I say it straight—staining the honor of a soldier?'
'That kind of sweet talk would be fine coming from this sixteen-year-old count here,' said Dolokhov with cold irony. 'But it's time you dropped it.'
'I haven't said anything! I only said I'm definitely going with you,' said Petya timidly.

'But for you and me, old man, it's time to drop these niceties,' Dolokhov continued, seeming to enjoy the topic that irritated Denisov. 'Why have you kept this boy?' he went on, shaking his head. 'Because you feel sorry for him! Don't we all know about your "receipts"? You send off a hundred and thirty arrive. The rest either starve or get killed. So what's the difference?'
The esaul nodded approvingly, squinting his light-colored eyes.
'That's beside the point. I'm not going to debate it. I refuse to have it on my conscience. You say they'll die. Fine. But not because of me!'
Dolokhov laughed.

'Who's told them not to capture me these twenty times over? But if they did catch me, they'd string me up on an aspen tree, and all your chivalry wouldn't make a bit of difference.' He paused. 'Anyway, we need to get moving. Tell the Cossack to fetch my kit. I've got two French uniforms in it. So—are you coming with me?' he asked Petya.
'I? Yes, yes, absolutely!' cried Petya, blushing almost to tears and glancing at Denisov.

While Dolokhov had been arguing with Denisov about what to do with prisoners, Petya had again felt awkward and restless—but once more he didn't have time to fully grasp what they were discussing. 'If grown-up, distinguished men think this way, it must be necessary and right,' he thought. 'But above all, Denisov must not dare think I'll just obey him and let him order me around. I will definitely go to the French camp with Dolokhov. If he can do it, so can I!'
And to all Denisov's attempts to dissuade him, Petya replied that he too was in the habit of doing everything precisely, not 'just anyhow,' and that he never worried about personal danger.

'Because you have to admit—if we don't know exactly how many there are, hundreds of lives could depend on it, and there are only the two of us. Besides, I really want to go, and I'm definitely going. So please don't try to stop me,' he said. 'It will only make things worse.'

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter IX
paragraphs: Having put on French greatcoats and shakos, Petya and Dolokhov rode to the clearing from which Denisov had surveyed the French camp. Emerging from the forest into pitch darkness, they descended into the hollow. At the bottom, Dolokhov told the Cossacks accompanying him to wait there and rode on at a quick trot toward the bridge. Petya, his heart pounding with excitement, rode beside him.
'If we're caught, I won't be taken alive! I have a pistol,' he whispered.
'Don't speak Russian,' said Dolokhov in a hurried whisper, and at that very moment came the challenge from the darkness: 'Who goes there?' and the click of a musket.
('Who goes there?')
The blood rushed to Petya's face and he gripped his pistol.
'Lancers of the Sixth!' Dolokhov replied, neither quickening nor slowing his horse's pace.
('Lancers of the Sixth Regiment.')
The black shape of a sentinel stood on the bridge.
'Password.'
('Password.')
Dolokhov reined in his horse and walked it forward.
'Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?' he asked.
('Tell me, is Colonel Gerard here?')
'Password,' the sentinel repeated, blocking the way without answering.
'When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password!' Dolokhov suddenly barked, riding straight at the sentinel. 'I'm asking you if the colonel is here!'
('When an officer is making his rounds, sentinels don't ask for the password. I'm asking you if the colonel is here.')
And without waiting for an answer from the sentinel, who had stepped aside, Dolokhov rode up the slope at a walk.

Noticing the dark outline of a man crossing the road, Dolokhov stopped him and asked where the commander and officers were. The man—a soldier with a sack over his shoulder—stopped, came close to Dolokhov's horse, touched it with his hand, and explained simply and in a friendly way that the commander and officers were up the hill to the right, in the courtyard of the farm (as he called the landowner's house).

Having ridden up the road with French conversation audible around campfires on both sides, Dolokhov turned into the courtyard of the landowner's house. He dismounted and approached a large, blazing campfire around which several men sat talking noisily. Something was boiling in a small cauldron at the fire's edge, and a soldier in a peaked cap and blue overcoat, lit up by the flames, was kneeling beside it stirring the contents with a ramrod.
'Oh, he's a tough one,' said one of the officers sitting in the shadow on the other side of the fire.
'He'll make those fellows get a move on!' said another, laughing.
Both fell silent, peering into the darkness at the sound of Dolokhov's and Petya's footsteps approaching with their horses.
'Good evening, gentlemen!' Dolokhov said loudly and clearly.
('Good evening, gentlemen.')
There was a stir among the officers in the shadows, and one tall, long-necked officer walked around the fire toward Dolokhov.
'Is that you, Clement?' he asked. 'Where the devil—?' But catching his mistake, he broke off and, with a frown, greeted Dolokhov as a stranger, asking what he could do for him.

Dolokhov said that he and his companion were trying to catch up with their regiment and, addressing the group, asked whether anyone knew anything about the Sixth Regiment. No one knew anything. Petya thought the officers were beginning to eye him and Dolokhov with hostility and suspicion. For several seconds, no one spoke.
'If you were hoping for the evening soup, you've come too late,' said a voice from behind the fire, with a suppressed laugh.
Dolokhov replied that they weren't hungry and had to keep moving through the night.

He handed the horses to the soldier stirring the pot and squatted on his heels by the fire next to the long-necked officer, who kept staring at him and again asked what regiment he belonged to. Dolokhov, as if he hadn't heard, didn't answer. Instead, lighting a short French pipe he'd taken from his pocket, he began asking the officer how safe the road ahead was from Cossack attacks.
'Those bandits are everywhere,' replied an officer from behind the fire.

Dolokhov observed that Cossacks were only dangerous to lone stragglers like himself and his companion, 'but surely they wouldn't dare attack large detachments?' he added, as if seeking confirmation. No one responded.
'Well, now he'll leave,' Petya thought every moment as he stood by the fire listening.

But Dolokhov picked up the dropped conversation and began asking direct questions: how many men in the battalion, how many battalions, how many prisoners? Asking about the Russian prisoners in their column, Dolokhov said:

'Terrible nuisance dragging those corpses around! Better to shoot that rabble,' and he burst into such loud, strange laughter that Petya was sure the French would see through their disguise at any second. He involuntarily stepped back from the fire.

No one responded to Dolokhov's laughter. A French officer they couldn't see—lying wrapped in a greatcoat—sat up and whispered something to a companion. Dolokhov stood, called for the soldier holding their horses.
'Will they bring the horses, or won't they?' thought Petya, instinctively moving closer to Dolokhov.
The horses were brought.
'Good evening, gentlemen,' said Dolokhov.

Petya wanted to say 'Good night' but couldn't get the words out. The officers were whispering together. Dolokhov took a long time mounting his horse, which wouldn't stand still, then he rode out of the yard at a walk. Petya rode beside him, longing to look back to see if the French were following but not daring to.

Coming out onto the road, Dolokhov didn't ride back across the open ground but through the village. At one spot he stopped and listened. 'Do you hear?' he asked. Petya recognized the sound of Russian voices and saw the dark shapes of Russian prisoners huddled around their campfires. When they descended to the bridge, Petya and Dolokhov rode past the sentinel, who paced silently and morosely up and down, then dropped into the hollow where the Cossacks were waiting.
'Well then, goodbye. Tell Denisov: at the first shot, at daybreak,' said Dolokhov and was about to ride off, but Petya grabbed his arm.
'Really!' he cried. 'You're such a hero! Oh, how wonderful, how splendid! How I love you!'

'All right, all right!' said Dolokhov. But Petya wouldn't let go, and through the gloom Dolokhov saw him leaning forward, wanting to kiss him. Dolokhov kissed him, laughed, wheeled his horse around, and vanished into the darkness.

chapters.title: Book Fourteen (1812) — Chapter X
paragraphs: Returning to the watchman's hut, Petya found Denisov waiting in the passage. He'd been pacing with agitation, anxiety, and self-reproach for having let Petya go.

'Thank God!' he exclaimed. 'Yes, thank God!' he repeated, listening to Petya's rapturous account. 'But damn you, I couldn't sleep because of you! Well, thank God. Now lie down. We can still get some rest before morning.'
'But... no,' said Petya. 'I don't want to sleep yet. Besides, I know myself—if I fall asleep, that's the end. And anyway, I'm used to not sleeping before a battle.'
He sat in the hut for a while, happily reliving the details of his adventure and vividly imagining what would happen the next day.
Then, noticing that Denisov had fallen asleep, he got up and went outside.

It was still pitch dark. The rain had stopped, but drops were still falling from the trees. Near the watchman's hut, the dark shapes of the Cossacks' shelters and tethered horses could just be made out. Behind the hut, the dark outlines of two wagons with their horses beside them were barely visible, and in the hollow, the dying campfire glowed red. Not all the Cossacks and hussars were asleep; here and there, amid the sound of falling drops and horses munching nearby, low voices could be heard, seeming to whisper.

Petya stepped out, peered into the darkness, and walked over to the wagons. Someone was snoring underneath them, and saddled horses stood around, munching oats. In the dark, Petya recognized his own horse, which he called 'Karabakh' though it was actually a Ukrainian breed, and went up to it.
'Well, Karabakh! We'll see some action tomorrow,' he said, sniffing its nostrils and kissing it.
'Why aren't you asleep, sir?' asked a Cossack sitting under one of the wagons.
'No... Likhachev—that's your name, isn't it? You know, I've only just gotten back! We went right into the French camp.'
And Petya gave the Cossack a detailed account not only of his ride but also of his reasons, and why he thought it was better to risk his life than to do things 'just anyhow.'
'Well, you should get some sleep now,' said the Cossack.
'No, I'm used to this,' said Petya. 'By the way—are the flints in your pistols worn out? I brought some with me. Don't you want any? You can have some.'
The Cossack leaned forward from under the wagon to get a better look at Petya.
'Because I'm in the habit of doing everything precisely,' said Petya. 'Some people do things carelessly, without preparation, and then they're sorry. I don't like that.'
'That's for sure,' said the Cossack.
'Oh yes, one more thing! Please, my dear fellow, will you sharpen my saber? It's gotten bl—' (Petya was afraid to lie; the saber had never been sharpened.) 'Can you do it?'
'Of course.'
Likhachev got up, rummaged in his pack, and soon Petya heard the warlike sound of steel on whetstone. He climbed onto the wagon and sat on its edge. The Cossack was sharpening the saber underneath.
'Are the lads asleep?' asked Petya.
'Some are, some aren't—same as us.'
'And what about that boy?'
'Vesenny? Oh, he threw himself down there in the passage. Fast asleep after his fright. He was so happy!'
After that, Petya sat quietly for a long time, listening to the sounds. He heard footsteps in the darkness, and a black figure appeared.
'What are you sharpening?' asked the man, coming up to the wagon.
'This gentleman's saber.'
'That's good,' said the man, whom Petya took to be a hussar. 'Was the cup left here?'
'There, by the wheel.'
The hussar took the cup.
'Must be nearly daylight,' he said, yawning, and walked away.

Petya should have known that he was in a forest with Denisov's guerrilla band, less than a mile from the road, sitting on a wagon captured from the French; that under it Likhachev was sharpening his saber; that the big dark blotch to the right was the watchman's hut and the red blotch below to the left was the dying campfire; that the man who came for the cup was a hussar who wanted a drink. But he neither knew nor cared to know any of this. He was in a fairy kingdom where nothing resembled reality. The big dark blotch might be the watchman's hut, or it might be a cavern leading to the very depths of the earth. The red spot might be a fire, or the eye of an enormous monster. Maybe he really was sitting on a wagon, but it might just as easily be a terrifyingly high tower, and if he fell he'd keep falling for a whole day or a whole month, and never reach the bottom. Maybe it was just the Cossack Likhachev sitting under the wagon, but it might be the kindest, bravest, most wonderful man in the world—someone no one knew about. Maybe the hussar really had come for water and gone back to the hollow, but maybe he had simply vanished, dissolved into nothingness.
Nothing Petya might have seen now would have surprised him. He was in a fairy kingdom where everything was possible.

He looked up at the sky. And the sky was a fairy realm too, like the earth. It was clearing, and clouds sailed swiftly over the treetops as if unveiling the stars. Sometimes it looked as if the clouds were moving and a clear black sky showed between them. Sometimes the black spaces seemed to be clouds. Sometimes the sky appeared to rise incredibly high overhead; then it seemed to drop so low you could touch it with your hand.
Petya's eyes began to close and he swayed slightly.
The trees were dripping. Quiet talk was heard. The horses neighed and jostled. Someone snored.

'Ozheg-zheg, ozheg-zheg...' hissed the saber against the whetstone, and suddenly Petya heard a harmonious orchestra playing some unknown, sweetly solemn hymn. Petya was as musical as Natasha, and more so than Nikolai, but he had never studied music or thought about it, so the melody that came unexpectedly to his mind seemed to him especially fresh and beautiful. The music grew louder and richer, the melody passing from one instrument to another. What was being played was a fugue—though Petya had no idea what a fugue was. Each instrument—now sounding like a violin, now like a horn, but better and purer than either—played its own part, and before it had finished, another instrument took up almost the same melody, then a third and a fourth joined in. They all blended into one and then separated again, now merging into solemn church music, now into something dazzlingly brilliant and triumphant.
'Oh—wait, that was a dream!' Petya said to himself, lurching forward. 'It's in my ears. But maybe it's music of my own. Well, go on, my music! Play on!...'

He closed his eyes. From all sides, as if from a distance, sounds fluttered, swelled into harmonies, separated, and blended again into the same sweet, solemn hymn. 'Oh, this is wonderful! As much as I want, and however I want!' Petya said to himself. He tried to conduct that enormous orchestra.

'Now softer, softer—die away!' And the sounds obeyed him. 'Now fuller, more joyful! Still more, more joyful!' And from some unknown depth, increasingly triumphant sounds rose. 'Now voices, join in!' Petya ordered. And from far away he heard first men's voices, then women's. The voices swelled in harmonious, triumphant power, and Petya listened in awe and joy.

With the solemn, triumphant march there mingled the song of the dripping trees, the hissing of the saber—'Ozheg-zheg-zheg...'—and again the horses jostled and neighed, not breaking the music but joining it.
Petya didn't know how long this lasted. He savored every moment, marveling at his own delight and regretting there was no one to share it. He was woken by Likhachev's kind voice.
'It's ready, your honor. You could split a Frenchman in half with it!'
Petya woke up.
'It's getting light—it's really getting light!' he exclaimed.

The horses, previously invisible, could now be seen right down to their tails, and a watery light filtered through the bare branches. Petya shook himself, jumped up, pulled a ruble from his pocket and gave it to Likhachev, then flourished the saber, tested it, and sheathed it. The Cossacks were untying their horses and tightening saddle girths.
'Here comes the commander,' said Likhachev.
Denisov came out of the watchman's hut and, calling Petya over, gave orders to get ready.
